The Hawai`i `akepa (Loxops coccineus) is a small Hawaiian honeycreeper endemic to the island of Hawai`i, where it inhabits high-elevation mesic and wet forests dominated by koa and `ohi`a. Neonates at hatching are altricial, requiring intensive brooding, and based on data from the closely related Chlorodrepanis flava, the estimated wet weight at birth is approximately 1.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.2 grams], a value consistent with the tiny hatchling masses observed across the Hawaiian honeycreeper radiation. Eggs are laid in clutches of 1 to 2 [N_R_i = 1 to 2], and females typically produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward high individual offspring survival rather than high fecundity. The incubation period, which concludes with the emergence of the hatchling and its first exogenous feeding, lasts 15 days at an average nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]; this age at birth of 15 days [ab = 15 days] is characteristic of many passerine honeycreepers with similar egg sizes.

Once the altricial nestling emerges from the incubated egg, it enters a period of rapid growth and feather development within the nest cavity. Under the thermal conditions that prevail during the active breeding season (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), the fledging stage, defined as the time since birth at which the young bird achieves its first flight and departs the nest, occurs at approximately 18 days [tx = approximately 18 days]. This developmental milestone marks the transition from a completely dependent nestling to a fledgling that, while still reliant on parental provisioning for some time, can begin to explore the immediate vicinity of the nest. The body mass of the adults at this stage, which represents the ultimate wet weight the species attains, reaches approximately 10.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 10.4 grams]; this modest size is typical of insectivorous and nectarivorous honeycreepers and facilitates agile foraging in the canopy.

Sexual maturity in the Hawai`i `akepa, defined as the onset of puberty and the capacity to engage in reproductive activity, is reached 54 days after birth [tp = 54 days after birth] when the juvenile bird is maintained under typical active-season thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of puberty, compared to larger-bodied passerines, allows the species to potentially breed within the same season in which it hatched, a strategy that may be advantageous in the unpredictable environment of montane Hawaiian forests. The pre-reproductive juvenile period is characterized by continued refinement of foraging skills, as the young birds learn to extract insect larvae, spiders, and nectar from the bark and flowers of koa and `ohi`a. The development of the characteristic crossed mandible, used for prying open leaf buds, is gradually perfected during this sub-adult phase. This morphological adaptation is critical for accessing the arthropod prey that forms a substantial portion of the species' diet.

While puberty occurs relatively early, the age at first reproduction, or the time since birth at which a female produces her first brood, is considerably deferred. First successful breeding events in the Hawai`i `akepa have been recorded at 365 days after birth [tR = 365 days after birth], coinciding with the return of favorable nesting conditions in the following breeding season under the same ambient thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between the attainment of sexual maturity and actual first reproduction is common among small passerines, as it allows individuals to establish territories, secure a mate, and acquire the body condition necessary for the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The interval between hatching and first nesting thus represents a critical period of social and physiological preparation during which the immature bird transitions from a dispersive juvenile to a reproductively viable, territory-holding adult.

Maximum recorded longevity in the wild for the Hawai`i `akepa, based on banding studies and recapture data, is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Among the Hawaiian honeycreepers, this species exhibits one of the longer lifespans for a passerine of its diminutive size, a pattern often attributed to the low predation pressure and stable food resources found in isolated oceanic island ecosystems. The maximum reproductive rate implied by the species' fecundity schedule, given a clutch of 1 to 2 eggs and a single annual nesting attempt, translates to a maximum of 1 to 2 offspring per female per year [Ri = 1 to 2 offspring per female per year], a rate among the lowest recorded for the family Fringillidae. Natural mortality in adult birds is often associated with the progressive deterioration of physiological function linked to senescence and the exhaustion of lipid stores during periods of resource scarcity. The post-reproductive phase of life, though seldom observed in free-living populations, may see older individuals acting as auxiliary helpers at the nests of related breeders, a cooperative behavior documented in several other Hawaiian honeycreepers.
